events.text: You wake in a body that has not yet lost anything, and you remember losing it. The Hollow Dao. The Unborn on the passages. The houses of that life going out like lamps in a row. Nobody here has heard the names. The sky is ordinary and blue, and the tea is hot, and you are the only one in all the heavens who knows it is borrowed.

choices.text: Begin now: write down every name you remember

effects.log: You write until the ink runs out. Six commanders, five ancestors, one hollow. The list goes under your pillow.

choices.text: Drink the tea first. It may be the last calm cup

effects.log: You drink it slowly. It is very good tea, and you remember that it was the last time too.

events.text: A herald of your temple reads the year's prayers aloud, and one of them is the same prayer, word for word, that a child spoke the morning the Long Well broke. You stop the herald. You ask the child's village. It is still there, of course. It is still there.

choices.text: Send a god of your house to watch that village

effects.log: A watcher goes down the Well with orders that sound strange to everyone but you. The village is watched.

choices.text: Keep the prayer, and answer it yourself

effects.log: You answer it: rain for a dry field. The child will never know why the god looked so long at their name.

events.text: You find yourself counting the steps of the Stair of Clouds on the way down to a feast, and you know the exact one where Ashkel the Unweeping planted his white parasol. You stand on it. It is only marble. A passing immortal asks if you are well, and you say yes, because there is no way to say the rest.

choices.text: Have the step warded, quietly, at your own cost

effects.log: Masons come at night. The step is warded with old lines that no one will ask about for a long time.

choices.text: Go on down to the feast

effects.log: You go down. You laugh in the right places. Under the table your hand will not stop being a fist.

events.text: The first time you lost, you were slow. You remember that more than the rest: the letters you did not send, the gods you did not trust, the years you spent on a domain dispute while the Hollow Dao was already tasting the edges. Here is the domain dispute again, on your desk, in the same hand.

choices.text: Settle the dispute in a day, and spend the years on the passages

effects.log: You give up more than you have to. The other god is astonished. You are already reading maps of the Well.

choices.text: Fight the dispute properly this time, and win it

effects.log: You win it in a season. It is a real victory, and it feels like a small one.

events.text: A god you once watched die on the Maker's Thread sits across from you at a council, alive and bored, picking at a sleeve. You remember the exact words they said at the end. You find you cannot look at them without saying something, so you say good morning, very warmly, and they look at you as though you are strange.

choices.text: Tell them the truth, as much as they will hear

effects.log: They hear a little. They do not believe it. They do, at least, start keeping a sword by the bed.

choices.text: Say nothing, and simply be kind to them

effects.log: You are kind to them for years. They decide you are an odd friend, and keep you.

events.text: Your dreams are full of a sound like a ledger being closed. Karrow Who Counts, you think, half awake, and then you are fully awake and alone in a hall where no one has ever heard the name. You lie there until the lamps burn down, adding up what you lost the first time, and arriving at the same sum every way you try.

choices.text: Get up and start a ledger of your own: every ward, every ally

effects.log: By dawn your ledger is longer than Karrow's ever was. It is a beginning.

choices.text: Go back to sleep. The sum will keep

effects.log: You sleep badly, and it keeps. In the morning you are kinder to your servants than they can explain.

events.text: You know the shape of the year the first breach comes, the way a farmer knows a frost in the bones. It is not this year. It is soon. You walk your temples and find them full of ordinary prayers for ordinary things, and you hear in each one a person who has no idea how much you would give to keep them bored.

choices.text: Answer every prayer you can this year

effects.log: You answer more prayers in a year than in the last century. The faithful are puzzled, and grateful.

choices.text: Ask your faithful for wards instead of offerings

effects.log: The temples carve wards over their doors. They think it is a new fashion. It is a wall.

events.text: Somewhere in your memory a house of this life is already gone: its gate open, its lamps out, a name on a tablet that nobody lights. Here it stands, loud and alive, its people arguing over a wedding. You stand in its courtyard unseen for an hour, learning it by heart in case you are wrong about being able to save it.

choices.text: Make a promise to the courtyard, and begin

effects.log: You promise. Promises from gods are heavy things. You feel this one settle on your shoulders like a yoke.

choices.text: Go to the wedding, in disguise, and dance

effects.log: You dance badly and happily. Nobody guesses. The bride says you have the look of an old friend.

events.text: You go to the edge of the Divine Realm, to the place where the first crack will open, and you sit there for a while with your back against the sky. It is quiet. It is quieter than it has any right to be. Somewhere past it, you know, Ashkel is folding a letter and the Twins are arguing over whose turn it is to burn.

choices.text: Mark the place, and set wards no one else would think to

effects.log: You set the wards. It takes a year of your strength. The edge of the sky hums faintly now, like a held breath.

choices.text: Speak to the quiet. Tell it you are coming

effects.log: You tell it. Nothing answers. You feel, for no reason, that something on the other side has turned its head.

events.text: A young god newly raised asks you, as the young do, what the hardest thing you ever did was. You open your mouth to say a duel, a domain, a heart demon. What comes out is: 'Losing, and coming back to the morning before.' The young god laughs, thinking it a riddle. You laugh with them.

choices.text: Take the young god as a student, and teach them the passages

effects.log: You teach them to hold a narrow place. They think it is an odd syllabus. They learn it well.

choices.text: Let it stay a riddle

effects.log: It stays a riddle. Years later they will remember it, and understand, and come looking for you.

events.text: It begins as a sound below hearing, like a great door in a far house. Then the sky at the edge of the Divine Realm splits along a line as clean as a fold in paper, and through it you see nothing, which is worse than anything. Something has eaten the stars on the other side. A messenger of the Heavenly Dao reaches you first: the Unborn have come, and the passages down are open.

choices.text: Go to the crack yourself, now

effects.log: You go. It is colder there than any place has a right to be. You stand at it until the other gods arrive and find you already waiting.

choices.text: Call every god you know to council

effects.log: The council is loud and frightened and late. It is also, by the end, a council of war.

events.text: Your temples go quiet in the middle of a prayer, all at once, as if someone had put a hand over the world's mouth. Then the bells start on their own. Far out at the rim of the heavens a gate that was never built is opening, and through it walk shapes that were gods once, of a place that is not a place any more. The Heavenly Dao speaks your name, which it has never done.

choices.text: Answer the Heavenly Dao: you will stand

effects.log: You answer. A weight comes down on you that is not a burden, exactly. It is more like being counted.

choices.text: Go first to your temples and calm the faithful

effects.log: You go down to the bells and still them one by one. The faithful look up at you as though you were the sky.

events.text: A god of the Green Assembly comes to your hall at night, which no god does, and sits down without being asked. Their hands are grey to the wrist. 'They ate my grove,' they say, quite calmly, 'in an afternoon. The Hollow Dao, they call it. Its gods are the Unborn. They have found the passages.' Then they ask for water, and you see they have been crying for some time.

choices.text: Give them water, and listen to all of it

effects.log: You listen until dawn. By then you know the names of three Unborn, and the grove god is asleep in your chair.

choices.text: Go at once to the grove, to see

effects.log: The grove is a field of grey stalks that do not move in the wind. You stand in it, and understand the war.

events.text: On the edge of the sky a white parasol has opened. Under it a figure in grey sits at a small table with a pot of something steaming, as if waiting for a friend who is late. Behind it the dark goes back forever. The figure sees you, rises, and bows with great courtesy. 'Ashkel,' he says. 'I am so sorry about your world.' The Unborn have come.

choices.text: Bow back. Courtesy costs nothing yet

effects.log: You bow. Ashkel smiles as at a good student. Neither of you sits down.

choices.text: Tell him the world is not yet sorry for anything

effects.log: Ashkel inclines his head. 'Not yet,' he agrees, and pours a second cup that nobody will drink.

events.text: You knew. You have known for a whole life. Still, when the sky splits along the line you have watched for years, your heart stops as if it were the first time. The difference is this: the wards you set hum and hold for a breath, the gods you warned are already moving, and you are standing exactly where you need to stand.

choices.text: Give the orders you have rehearsed for a lifetime

effects.log: You give them in the order you wrote them. Gods who laughed at you are running to their posts.

choices.text: Look once at the crack, and remember the last time

effects.log: You remember. It hurts the way an old wound does in the cold. Then you turn your back on it and go to work.

events.text: The bells, then the silence, then the line in the sky. You count under your breath and the crack opens on the count, as it did. Gods around you cry out. You do not. Someone asks how you are so calm, and you say, honestly, that you have had time to get used to it. They look at you as one looks at a prophet or a madman.

choices.text: Send the warned gods to the passages at once

effects.log: They go. This time the passages have guards before the Unborn reach them, and a guard is half a wall.

choices.text: Tell the frightened god the truth: you have seen this

effects.log: They do not quite believe you. They stay close to you all day, which is a kind of belief.

events.text: Ashkel's parasol opens at the edge of the sky, on the hour, as it did. This time you are there first, with tea of your own. Ashkel stops, and looks at you for a long moment, and for the first time in all your memory of him something crosses that patient face that might be surprise. 'Have we met?' he asks. 'Once,' you say. 'You won.'

choices.text: Tell him that will not happen twice

effects.log: Ashkel studies you, then bows lower than before. 'Then I shall have to hurry,' he says. He sounds unused to the word.

choices.text: Pour him a cup, and say nothing else

effects.log: He sits, after a moment. You drink together on the edge of the end of the world. It is the strangest tea of your life.

events.text: A white parasol stands at the head of {og_passage}, and beneath it Ashkel the Unweeping takes his tea. His Unborn sit in rows behind him like guests at a long dinner. He sends you a letter, beautifully written, regretting the inconvenience. 'Your world was lovely,' it says. 'I have read about it.' The siege has begun, and he is in no hurry at all.

choices.text: Go down and knock the cup from his hand

ok.log: You cross the field in one breath. The cup breaks. Ashkel looks at the pieces, and then at you, with polite interest. His rows fall back a step.

fail.log: He moves his cup an inch. Your blow passes it. A dozen Unborn rise without haste and walk you back to your own line.

choices.text: Answer the letter in the same fine hand

effects.log: You write that the world is still lovely, and still yours. He replies within the hour, with a correction to your grammar.

choices.text: Dig in, and make him wait as long as he likes

effects.log: You dig in. Ashkel admires the earthworks aloud. The Heavenly Dao counts the days you hold.

events.text: Ashkel has had a pavilion built at {og_passage}, of grey cloth that does not move in the wind, and he has hung in it a painting of your world as seen from a great height. Under it is written, in small neat characters, a date. You understand after a moment that it is the day he expects to have finished. It is not soon. It is very certain.

choices.text: Burn the pavilion, painting and all

ok.log: It goes up like paper, which it is. Ashkel watches it burn with his hands folded, and moves his camp back a hill.

fail.log: You never reach it. His guests rise from their long table and close around you, courteous and immovable.

choices.text: Study the painting. Know what he thinks he has

effects.log: He has painted it well. He has also painted the passages, and one ward you thought was secret. You change it that night.

choices.text: Write a later date under his, in larger characters

effects.log: You write it. Ashkel sends a note: 'Ambitious.' You hang the note in your hall.

events.text: The Unborn under Ashkel do not charge. They advance one step a day, all together, and at each step they stop and bow. It is the most frightening thing you have seen in a thousand years. By the tenth day the front is a field's width closer. Your gods are not sleeping. Ashkel, you are told, sleeps very well.

choices.text: Break the line at the step, while they bow

ok.log: You strike on the bow. The line folds like a fan. For the first time Ashkel stands up from his table.

fail.log: They finish the bow and then turn, all together, and you are pressed back three steps for every one.

choices.text: Hold your own line one step closer every night

effects.log: You give back his patience. Night by night your line creeps forward. The Heavenly Dao notices.

choices.text: Sleep, and let them see you do it

effects.log: You sleep in the open, in plain sight. In the morning the Unborn are a step further off. Ashkel sends his compliments.

events.text: Ashkel's parasol is at the top of the Stair of Clouds, on the very step where the immortals of the Upper Realm come up to pray. They come anyway. He moves aside for them with a little bow, and wishes each one a good day, and tells them gently that they will not have many more. Some of them turn back down the Stair weeping. That is the point.

choices.text: Stand on the step yourself and push him off it

ok.log: You meet him on the marble. He gives ground with perfect grace, three steps, five, ten, and the pilgrims behind you start to sing.

fail.log: He does not give a step. You are put down on the marble as gently as a cup, and the pilgrims see it.

choices.text: Walk the pilgrims down yourself, one by one

effects.log: You walk every one of them down. It takes all night. Not one of them weeps again on the way.

choices.text: Set a ward across the Stair, and pay for it in years

effects.log: The ward holds. It costs you some of your years. The Heavenly Dao is not a miser about what it owes you.

events.text: Two figures come up {og_passage} like the two halves of a coin thrown hard. Ves burns gold and talks without stopping; Ru burns pale and does not talk at all. They were one sun once, of a world nobody remembers, and they quarrel about it the whole way up. 'You're slow.' 'You're loud.' 'You were always the slow half.' The Twins Who Were One Sun have come.

choices.text: Go between them, while they quarrel

ok.log: You step into the gap between the halves. Both of them stop arguing at once, which is how you know you hurt them.

fail.log: They close the gap together, and for one terrible moment they are one sun again. You come back to your line with your sleeves smoking.

choices.text: Listen to the quarrel. It may tell you something

effects.log: It tells you a great deal. Ves blames Ru for the death of their world. Ru blames no one, which Ves cannot bear.

choices.text: Hold the narrow place and let them argue

effects.log: You hold. They argue. The front does not move all day, and the Heavenly Dao keeps the count.

events.text: Ru comes alone to the edge of your lines at dusk, pale fire low in the grass, and says the first words you have ever heard from that half: 'If you have to put one of us out, let it be me.' Then Ru is gone, back to the Unborn camp, where you can hear Ves shouting about something, and laughing, and shouting again.

choices.text: Keep the request to yourself

effects.log: You keep it. In the next fight you find yourself watching which half is which.

choices.text: Follow Ru back, and strike the camp

ok.log: You hit the camp before Ves has stopped laughing. The Twins pull back down the passage, arguing about whose fault it was.

fail.log: Ves sees you first. The laugh stops. You are driven back by a heat that feels personal.

choices.text: Use the dusk: move your line up while Ves is loud

effects.log: Ves is too loud to hear you move. By morning your line is a hill closer, and the Heavenly Dao has seen it.

events.text: Ves stands on a rock at {og_passage} and makes a speech to your gods about how small they are. It is a good speech. Halfway through, Ru, behind, quietly corrects a date in it, and Ves stops, and turns, and the two of them argue for an hour in front of both armies while the sun goes down. Your gods begin, slowly, to laugh.

choices.text: Charge while the Unborn are watching their masters

ok.log: You charge in the middle of the argument. The Twins stop only when your line is past the rock. The laughter on your side is very loud.

fail.log: The Twins stop arguing the moment you move. Two suns look at you at once. You go back carrying a god who was too slow.

choices.text: Let your gods laugh. They need it

effects.log: They laugh until the Unborn line shifts uneasily. A laughing army is hard to frighten.

events.text: The Twins come down the Maker's Thread into the world your soul once made, and its little gods run from them like sparrows from a fire. Ves sets a mountain alight to see it burn. Ru, behind, puts it out again without a word. You do not know yet what to make of that. You know the Thread is yours, and they are on it.

choices.text: Meet them on the Thread, before they reach the bottom

ok.log: You meet them halfway down. The Thread hums under three suns' worth of heat and holds, and the Twins go back up it quarrelling.

fail.log: The Thread sways. You catch it and hold it and they pass you, and the world you made sees two suns in its sky.

choices.text: Shelter the little gods first, then fight

effects.log: You gather the little gods in your sleeves like birds. The Heavenly Dao counts each one.

choices.text: Watch Ru put out the fires, and remember it

effects.log: You watch. Ru puts out every fire Ves lights, one after another, and never says a word.

events.text: The prayers rising up {og_passage} start to come thin, then late, then not at all. Somewhere on the way something is eating them. When you go to look, there is a soft grey shape on the passage the size of a temple, folding and unfolding its wings, and a voice like a grandmother's says, 'Oh, there you are, dear. Come and sit. I was only having a little something.' Old Moth has come.

choices.text: Strike her wings while she eats

ok.log: Grey dust fills the passage. Old Moth tuts at you as at a child who has knocked over the soup, and flutters back.

fail.log: She folds a wing over you, very gently. When it opens you are back at your own line and a little older in the face.

choices.text: Pray yourself, loud, straight up the passage

effects.log: Your prayer goes past her like a stone through cloth. She coughs. 'Too sharp, dear,' she says. 'Much too sharp.'

choices.text: Carry the prayers up by hand, past her

effects.log: You carry the prayers in your own arms, all night. Old Moth watches you go by, sorrowfully, like a cook watching a meal go to the neighbours.

events.text: Old Moth has got into one of your temples on the far side of {og_passage}. The faithful there say a kind old woman came in out of the rain, and sat in the back, and listened to their prayers with her eyes closed. After she left, none of them could remember what they had been praying for. Some of them could not remember the god's name. Yours.

choices.text: Go to the temple, and drive her out

ok.log: She is in the rafters when you come, folded small. She goes out through the roof with a little cry, and the faithful remember your name.

fail.log: She is gone before you arrive, and two more temples have forgotten you before you leave.

choices.text: Teach the faithful your name again, one by one

effects.log: You stand in the temple and say your name to each of them like a friend. They remember. It is slow. It is worth it.

events.text: A child's prayer reaches you whole, which has not happened for months, and in it the child says that a grandmother in grey has been telling stories at the well every evening, and the stories are lovely, and afterwards nobody prays. Old Moth is not fighting your gods. She is being kind to your faithful, and starving you.

choices.text: Go down and face her at the well

ok.log: You meet her at the well among the sleeping children. She looks at you, and for a moment seems truly sad. Then she is gone.

fail.log: She tells you a story. It is lovely. When you come back to yourself, three nights have passed and the front has moved.

choices.text: Tell the children a better story yourself

effects.log: You sit by the well and tell them how the gods held the passages. They pray again that night. The Heavenly Dao listens.

choices.text: Thank the child for the prayer, and answer it

effects.log: The child asked for a good harvest. You give one. It is small, and it is loud, and Old Moth cannot eat a harvest.

events.text: Old Moth sits in the mouth of the Long Well itself, where the mortal world's prayers come up like smoke from a thousand chimneys, and eats them as they rise. Below, in the world of mortals, people are kneeling in temples and feeling, for no reason, that no one is listening. They are right. You can feel their prayers going out like sparks in rain.

choices.text: Drag her out of the Well by the wings

ok.log: You haul her out into the open sky. Her voice goes thin and querulous. Below, a whole province of prayers comes up at once.

fail.log: The Well is narrow and she is everywhere in it. You come out grey to the elbows, and the prayers stay quiet.

choices.text: Go down the Well and answer prayers from below

effects.log: You go down among the mortals and answer what you can, by hand. It is beneath you. It feeds no moth.

choices.text: Light the Well with your own faith, and hold it

effects.log: You burn your own faith like a lamp in the Well's throat. She will not come near the flame.

events.text: At {og_passage} there is a desk. At the desk sits Karrow Who Counts, in a coat of many pockets, writing in a ledger as long as a road. Each page is a world. Most are crossed out. Karrow looks up at you over a pair of small spectacles and says, 'Ah. Good. I was just valuing you,' and goes on writing. The Unborn behind the desk wait for the sum.

choices.text: Overturn the desk

ok.log: The ledger goes flying. Pages of dead worlds fall like snow across the passage, and Karrow scrambles after them, and the Unborn have no orders for an hour.

fail.log: Karrow steps aside without looking up, and the desk does not move. Something in the ledger has a line under your name now.

choices.text: Ask what Karrow has written down for you

effects.log: Karrow shows you. It is a very precise number. It is not flattering. You learn exactly what the Hollow Dao wants first.

choices.text: Hold the passage while Karrow does the sums

effects.log: You hold all day. At dusk Karrow sighs, crosses something out, and starts the page again. The Heavenly Dao counts too.

events.text: Karrow sends you a contract, in triplicate. It proposes that the Hollow Dao take {og_passage} now, cleanly, and leave the rest of your heavens for a further thousand years. It lists what you would save, by number, and what you would lose, by number. It is very fair. It is the fairest offer you have ever read, and it is still a world.

choices.text: Tear it up, all three copies

effects.log: You tear them up. Karrow writes back to ask whether you would like the copies replaced. You do not answer.

choices.text: Take the contract back to Karrow in person, and refuse it to the face

ok.log: You hand it back across the desk and then put your fist through the desk. Karrow sighs and moves the camp back to make room for a new one.

fail.log: Karrow takes the contract and stamps it 'Declined', and the Unborn come forward at once, as if the stamp had been their signal.

choices.text: Read it again, slowly, to see what Karrow fears

effects.log: Line nine covers the case where you hold for a century. Karrow has priced it very high. You decide to hold for a century.

events.text: Karrow has a scale at {og_passage}, and on one pan is a little heap of grey ash that was once a world, and on the other is a bead of light that is your own. They balance exactly. 'You see,' Karrow says kindly, 'there is no difference. There never is. I have weighed nine thousand.' Then the Unborn begin to advance in the order of the ledger.

choices.text: Put your own weight on your world's pan

ok.log: You lay your hand on the pan. It goes down with a bang. Karrow stares at it, and takes off the spectacles, and polishes them for a long time.

fail.log: The pans do not move for you. Karrow writes something, and the Unborn come on in good order.

choices.text: Fight for a day in the order of his ledger, and wreck it

effects.log: You fight them in exactly the wrong order. By evening Karrow's ledger is a mess, and the Heavenly Dao has a fresh column of its own.

choices.text: Ask whose world the ash was

effects.log: Karrow tells you. It had a sea, and a festival of kites. Karrow remembers the kites. You did not expect that.

events.text: Karrow has set up shop at the top of the Stair of Clouds and is buying. Immortals of the Upper Realm come up the Stair and sell what they think little of: a few years, a name nobody uses, the colour of their eyes. Karrow pays in clean grey coin that is worth nothing at all, and writes each sale down, and the Stair grows a little thinner with every one.

choices.text: Shut the shop, and send the customers home

ok.log: You close the shutters with one hand and the Stair with the other. Karrow packs up, muttering about bad markets.

fail.log: The shop is open again behind you before you have walked away. The customers do not want to be saved.

choices.text: Buy back what the immortals sold, with your own fame

effects.log: You buy it back. It costs you a great deal of standing. The immortals get their names and eyes and years back, and some of them weep.

choices.text: Stand at the foot of the Stair and warn them off

effects.log: You warn them off for a season. The Stair stops thinning. The Heavenly Dao does not forget a season.

events.text: A figure in a long white veil walks up {og_passage}, and wherever she walks a door appears in the air, and opens on a room, and the room is empty. She looks into each one. She sighs. She walks on. The rooms stay behind her like shells on a beach. The Bride of Empty Rooms is looking for a home again, and she has started looking in yours.

choices.text: Close the doors behind her, one by one

ok.log: You close them as fast as she opens them. At the last one she turns, and the veil lifts a little, and she looks at you as if you had shut her out of a house she loved.

fail.log: There are too many doors. You close a hundred and she opens a thousand, and in one of them you find a room you knew.

choices.text: Look into one of the rooms yourself

effects.log: It is a kitchen. It is warm. There is a chair at the table as if someone had just got up. Nobody has ever sat there.

choices.text: Hold the passage; she can open doors but not walls

effects.log: You build walls as she opens doors. Behind each door is your wall. The Heavenly Dao counts them all.

events.text: The Bride stands at the edge of your lines at {og_passage} and asks your gods, one at a time, very softly, 'Is this your home? May I come in?' Some of them say no. One says yes, out of pity or out of fear, and you watch that god's hall empty itself like a room when a party ends: the furniture first, then the lamps, then the god.

choices.text: Stand between her and the next god she asks

ok.log: She asks you. You say no, and the no is a wall, and she steps back from it as if it burned. She does not ask anyone else that day.

fail.log: She asks you, and for a moment you cannot speak, and in that moment two more gods have said yes.

choices.text: Go to the emptied god's hall, and sit in it

effects.log: It is very quiet. You light one lamp in it. When you leave, it is still burning, and the hall is less empty for it.

events.text: There is a house on {og_passage} that was not there yesterday. It is a small house, with a red door and a crooked chimney, and the Bride of Empty Rooms is sitting on its step with her veil in her hands. Her Unborn stand around it in the dark. 'I nearly had it,' she says to you when you come, as though you were an old friend. 'I nearly did.'

choices.text: Knock the house down and drive her off the passage

ok.log: The house comes down like a card house, which it was. She does not fight you. She only walks away, and the doors open in the air behind her.

fail.log: Her Unborn close around the house as if it were a child. You are pushed back from it, and she watches you go with dry eyes.

choices.text: Sit on the step beside her for a while

effects.log: You sit. Neither of you says anything. After a time she gets up and goes, and leaves the house standing, and you leave it too.

choices.text: Leave the house; take back the rest of the passage

effects.log: You leave her the house and take everything around it. By morning it stands alone in your lines. The Heavenly Dao counts the ground.

events.text: The Bride has come down the Long Well into the mortal world, and in a town below the houses are emptying. Nobody is hurt. The people simply walk out of their doors one morning and do not remember why they lived there, and stand in the streets like guests at the end of a long party. The Bride walks from house to house, looking in, sighing.

choices.text: Go down and face her in the empty street

ok.log: You stand in the street between her and the next door. She looks at you a long while, and then turns back up the Well.

fail.log: She walks past you into the next house as though you were a draught. Another street empties.

choices.text: Lead the people back into their houses, one by one

effects.log: You go door to door and tell each family whose house it is. It is slow and it holds. She cannot eat a home that knows it is one.

choices.text: Ward the town's doors with your name

effects.log: Every door in the town has your mark on it by sundown. The Bride walks past and does not look in. The Heavenly Dao notes it.

events.text: The tide comes in up {og_passage}, which is not possible, and on it rides a tall god in grey armour with salt in his beard and a face that will not look at you. Thane Ulo of the Last Coast, the Unborn call him. He commands them well and without joy. When his tide reaches your line, he stops it, exactly at the line, and stands there in the surf as if waiting to be told something.

choices.text: Wade out and meet him in the surf

ok.log: You meet him knee-deep. He fights like a god who learned on a real shore, and gives way like one who does not want to win. The tide goes out.

fail.log: He is very strong and very tired, and the tired is no help to you. The tide carries you back to your line.

choices.text: Ask him what he is waiting for

effects.log: He does not answer. He looks at the shore behind you, at the shape of it, for a long time, and then his tide goes out.

choices.text: Hold the line he stopped at, and do not cross it

effects.log: You hold it. He holds his. The front does not move, and the Heavenly Dao counts the quiet.

events.text: At night, from the Unborn side of {og_passage}, someone is singing. It is a sailors' song, from a sea that does not exist any more, and it is Thane Ulo singing it, alone, to the dark. His Unborn do not sing. They do not know how. Your gods on watch listen until the song ends, and in the morning none of them wants to fight.

choices.text: Attack at dawn while the song is still in his voice

ok.log: You come at dawn. He fights you hoarse, and badly, and when you push him back he goes without a word.

fail.log: He has sung all night and still does not tire. You are pushed back with salt in your hair.

choices.text: Sing a song of your own world back

effects.log: You sing what you remember of a fishing song from the world below. On the other side the singing stops, and then, very low, takes up your tune.

choices.text: Use the night: move your line while they listen

effects.log: Your line moves while the Unborn stand listening to a song they cannot understand. The Heavenly Dao is not sentimental.

events.text: Thane Ulo sends you a gift across the field: a shell, grey as ash, the last shell of the Last Coast. With it is no message. His Unborn come on the next morning as hard as they ever have, and he is at the front of them, and he fights you as if he hoped you would win and would not forgive himself if he let you.

choices.text: Fight him as hard as he fights you

ok.log: You give him the fight he asked for. At the end of it he is on one knee, and the front is back a hill, and he thanks you.

fail.log: He wins the morning. He does not look pleased. He looks at the shell in your sash as he goes.

choices.text: Keep the shell, and hold back from killing blows

effects.log: You fight him carefully all morning. He notices. He fights you carefully back. Neither front moves an inch.

events.text: Ulo has brought his tide down the Maker's Thread into the world your soul once made, and that world has a sea, a small one, that you made long ago. He stops at its shore. He kneels and puts his hand in it. When he looks up at you across the water, the face that will not look at anyone is looking at you, and it is the face of a man at a grave.

choices.text: Strike while he kneels

ok.log: He does not defend himself until the last moment, and then not well. His tide goes back up the Thread, and he goes with it.

fail.log: He rises out of the water like the sea itself rising. You hold the shore, but only just, and the little sea runs grey for a day.

choices.text: Wait until he stands, and then fight

effects.log: You wait. He stands, and bows to you, and then fights like a sea-god. You win nothing that day, and lose nothing.

choices.text: Raise the little sea against his tide

effects.log: Your sea rises at your word and meets his. It is small, and it is home, and his tide will not climb it.

events.text: The great gathering of the heavens should be music and banners. Instead every god in the Divine Realm is on the walls, because on the day it opens {og_unborn} comes up {og_passage} with every Unborn of the field at once. It is not a siege any more. It is a tide. The gathering's banners are torn down to make bandages for gods.

choices.text: Lead the gathered gods down to meet it

ok.log: You lead them down. It is the loudest day the heavens have known. At dusk the tide is going out, and the gods carry you up the passage on their shoulders.

fail.log: You lead them down and the tide does not break. You bring back fewer than you took, and you count them all.

choices.text: Hold the walls; let it break itself on them

effects.log: It breaks on the walls all day and all night. The walls hold. The Heavenly Dao counts every stone.

choices.text: Send the young gods back to their halls first

effects.log: You send the young ones home. Some of them never forgive you. All of them live.

events.text: The gathering was to be the Contest of Pantheons, and the pantheons are all here, in their best, when the push comes. The four great halls look at one another across the field in the old way, measuring old grudges. Then they look at {og_passage}, where {og_unborn} has brought everything, and for the first time in an age the four of them stand on the same side.

choices.text: Fight at the front of all four pantheons

ok.log: All four pantheons see you take the first blow and give back three. By evening they are cheering one another, which has not happened in ten thousand years.

fail.log: You take the first blow and it is a great deal heavier than you thought. The pantheons carry you back, and argue about who carried you.

choices.text: Make the four pantheons swear to one another first

effects.log: You make them swear. It takes an hour you did not have. The oath holds through the whole push.

choices.text: Take the worst ground, the one no hall wants

effects.log: You take the ground nobody wants. You hold it. The Heavenly Dao sees who took it.

events.text: The Council of the Dao meets to argue the order of the stars, and the stars go out. One by one, over the passage, they are eaten, until the sky over {og_passage} is as dark as the gap between two words. Then the Unborn come down out of that dark in their thousands. {og_unborn} is at the head, and the Council stops arguing.

choices.text: Light the dark yourself, and fight by it

ok.log: You burn so bright the dark has edges again, and the gods can see what they are fighting. It is enough.

fail.log: You burn and the dark eats the light. You fight blind for a night, and lose ground, and keep your life.

choices.text: Turn the Council into a war council on the spot

effects.log: The Council has argued for a thousand years. It turns out it can also decide in an hour. You are proud of it.

choices.text: Guard the Council's hall until the push is done

effects.log: You stand at the Council's doors for three days. Nobody gets in. The Heavenly Dao counts the days.

events.text: A great gathering is a day the heavens show off. This one, the Unborn have chosen to show off back. On every passage at once they come up in ranks so wide they have no edge, and in the middle of the widest is {og_unborn}, larger than you have ever seen. Every god at the gathering is looking at you, you realise, because you have done this before.

choices.text: Go first. They will follow you

ok.log: You go first and they follow, a river of gods, and the ranks with no edge find an edge. It is you.

fail.log: You go first and they follow and the ranks do not break. You pull back in good order. In good order is something.

choices.text: Give the gods a plan, not a speech

effects.log: You give them a plan. It is short. They follow it. Most of them come home.

choices.text: Hold one passage alone, so the rest can hold two

effects.log: You take {og_passage} by yourself. It is the longest night of your life. The Heavenly Dao does not forget nights.

events.text: The gathering this age was to be a feast, and the feast is laid when the push comes: long tables in the clouds, gods in silk, cups poured. The Unborn come up {og_passage} so fast that the cups are still warm when the first ranks reach the tables. {og_unborn} picks one up, and drinks, and says it was very good, and sets it down.

choices.text: Throw the table at them, cups and all

ok.log: The table goes over like a wave and the Unborn are buried in silk and dishes. The gods fight with whatever is to hand, and win.

fail.log: The table goes over. So do you. The Unborn are very calm about broken dishes.

choices.text: Get every guest out, then fight

effects.log: You clear the feast first. Every guest gets out. The tables are lost. Tables are cheap.

choices.text: Fight from the high table, and keep the hall

effects.log: You hold the high table all night with a cup still in your hand. The Heavenly Dao enjoys it, you think.

events.text: This push is different: the Unborn are not coming up {og_passage}, they are coming up all of it, as if the passage were a throat and they were swallowing upward. The gods of the gathering stand in a ring around its mouth. {og_unborn} sends you one message before it begins. It says: 'Let us finish this properly.'

choices.text: Fight at the mouth, and finish it properly

ok.log: You finish it properly. When it is done the mouth of the passage is quiet, and you are the last god standing at its lip.

fail.log: You fight at the mouth and the throat keeps swallowing. You hold the lip, but the front has moved, and everyone can see it.

choices.text: Seal the ring of gods into a single ward

effects.log: You join every god's hands into one ward. It holds the passage shut while they push. The Heavenly Dao counts each hand.

events.text: The push comes on the eve of the gathering, when the Divine Realm is full of guests from every pantheon, and so it is the guests who die first. Not many: the Unborn are not wasteful. Enough. {og_unborn} has done it on purpose, to make the heavens quarrel over who brought it on them, and you can already hear the quarrel starting in the halls.

choices.text: Stop the push before the quarrel spreads

ok.log: You stop the push in a night. In the morning there is nothing to quarrel about but who fought best, and that quarrel is good for everyone.

fail.log: The push goes on, and the quarrel with it. You hold, but the halls are shouting at each other as well as at the Unborn.

choices.text: Stop the quarrel first. The push can wait an hour

effects.log: You go from hall to hall and say one thing: that this is what the Unborn want. It is true, and they hear it.

choices.text: Mourn the guests, openly, before you fight

effects.log: You stand in front of all the halls and grieve for the guests by name. Nobody quarrels in front of grief.

events.text: It is a quiet great gathering this age, a gathering of the old, where ancient gods come out of their long sleep to see the stars once. The Unborn come for them. {og_unborn} knows the old are slow to wake. On {og_passage}, in the starlight, gods older than the mountains of the Upper Realm are blinking at an enemy they do not understand.

choices.text: Fight in front of the old gods until they wake

ok.log: You fight long enough for the old to wake. When they wake, they wake all at once, and the Unborn learn why the heavens are old.

fail.log: You fight, and the old are slow, and you take every blow meant for them. They wake in the end. You do not remember that part.

choices.text: Wake the old gods yourself, one by one

effects.log: You wake them with their own names. Some of them have not heard their names in a hundred thousand years. They come up roaring.

choices.text: Carry the old gods off the passage

effects.log: You carry them like grandparents. They complain about it all the way. The Heavenly Dao counts each one.

events.text: Ashkel the Unweeping sits down on the step of {og_passage} very slowly, as an old man sits, and puts his cup to one side. 'Well,' he says. 'Well. That was not in my reading.' His rows fold up their long table and go back into the dark without being told. Before he follows, he writes you a short letter. It says only: 'Again.'

choices.text: Keep the letter, and answer it 'Gladly'

effects.log: You send the answer after him into the dark. You fancy you hear, very far off, a courteous little laugh.

choices.text: Use the hour: push the field back while he sits

effects.log: You push the field back while he sits. He watches you do it with something like approval.

events.text: Ashkel's parasol lies on the passage, torn. He picks it up and looks at the tear for a long while. 'In all the worlds,' he says, 'nobody has torn it.' He does not seem angry. He seems interested, as a scholar is interested in a book that has surprised him. 'Your world,' he says, 'may not be quite as eaten as I wrote.' Then he leaves.

choices.text: Ask him how many worlds he has written that about

effects.log: He tells you: all of them. Every world was eaten as he wrote. He looks at you as though wondering which kind you are.

choices.text: Chase his rows down the passage

effects.log: You chase them a long way. They do not run; they only walk, rather quickly. The front goes back with them.

events.text: Ves is down, gold fire guttering in the grass, and Ru, who never speaks, is kneeling over Ves and speaking: a stream of words in a dead star's language that you do not need to understand. Ves is telling Ru to go. Ru is not going. The Unborn behind them fall back from the two of them as if from a fire in the wrong place.

choices.text: Let them both go back, together

effects.log: You step back. Ru gathers up Ves like an armful of light and goes back down the passage. Neither looks at you.

choices.text: Drive the Unborn off while the Twins are down

effects.log: You drive the Unborn off the field. The Twins go last, arguing in whispers.

events.text: It is Ru who falls, pale fire scattered. Ves stands over the scatter, gold, roaring, and you brace for the worst blow of your life. It does not come. Ves only kneels and begins picking up the pieces of Ru one by one, and saying, 'You slow fool, you slow fool,' over and over, quite gently.

choices.text: Walk away. Leave Ves to it

effects.log: You walk away. Behind you the gold fire and the pale one are slowly becoming one fire again.

choices.text: Take the field while Ves is gathering

effects.log: You take the field. Nobody stops you. Ves is still gathering when you are done.

events.text: Old Moth is very small when she is beaten, a grey thing the size of a lamp-moth, and she sits on your sleeve with her wings folded. 'Oh, dear,' she says. 'Oh, you are a sharp one. I was only hungry.' Then she flutters off down {og_passage}, and behind her come all the prayers she ate, rising up in a great slow cloud.

choices.text: Catch the prayers and answer them all

effects.log: You catch them as they rise. There are years of them. You answer as many as a god can answer in a year.

choices.text: Blow her down the passage, with all her kind

effects.log: You blow, and the passage clears of grey like a window. The front goes back with them.

events.text: Old Moth sits on the step of a temple at the foot of {og_passage}, beaten, and the faithful come out and look at her, and do not know what she is. One of them, an old woman herself, brings out a bowl of rice. Old Moth looks at it for a long time. 'I don't eat that, dear,' she says. 'But thank you.' She goes, slowly, with the rice uneaten.

choices.text: Thank the old woman

effects.log: You thank her, in a dream that night. She tells everyone she met her god, and nobody believes her, and she does not care.

choices.text: Seal the temple behind Old Moth

effects.log: You seal the temple with the old woman's kindness, which is strong. Old Moth will not come back here.

events.text: Karrow's ledger is closed, and Karrow sits on the ground beside it, spectacles in hand. 'I made a mistake,' Karrow says, in a voice of real astonishment. 'I have never made a mistake. I priced you wrong.' The Unborn wait for an order that does not come. After a while Karrow gets up, dusts off the coat, and opens the ledger to a fresh page.

choices.text: Ask what Karrow writes on the fresh page

effects.log: Karrow shows you. It is your name, and next to it, for the first time in nine thousand worlds, a question mark.

choices.text: Clear the field while Karrow recounts

effects.log: You clear the field while Karrow is doing sums. Karrow does not look up once.

events.text: You win, and Karrow pays: that is the strange thing. Karrow takes out a small purse and counts into your hand the price of the defeat, in grey coin, exactly. 'I always settle,' Karrow says. 'It is the only thing I believe in.' The coins are worth nothing. They are very heavy. The Unborn pack up their desks and go back down {og_passage}.

choices.text: Keep the coins as a reminder

effects.log: You keep them in a box in your hall. On bad nights you take them out and weigh them in your hand.

choices.text: Throw the coins back down the passage

effects.log: You throw them after the Unborn. They fall a long way. Karrow, somewhere below, writes 'Refused' in the ledger.

events.text: The Bride of Empty Rooms stands still on {og_passage}, beaten, and all the doors she opened in the air begin, one after another, to close by themselves. She watches them close. She does not try to stop them. When the last is shut she says, without turning, 'None of them was home either,' and goes back into the dark.

choices.text: Call after her: what would a home look like?

effects.log: She stops. She does not answer. She goes. You find later that you have kept the question, as though for her.

choices.text: Follow the closing doors and take back the field

effects.log: You follow the doors closing and take back every room of ground they stood on.

events.text: You have beaten the Bride, and in beating her you have knocked her veil away. Under it is a face of no particular age, tired and plain, the face of someone who has been travelling a very long time. She covers it again with her hands. 'Please do not look,' she says. 'I was a bride once. There was a house.' Then she is gone.

choices.text: Look away, as she asked

effects.log: You look away. When you look back she is gone, and there is a single empty room in the air that slowly fades.

choices.text: Hold the field she has left

effects.log: You hold it. Behind you the gods are quiet, as if after a funeral.

events.text: Thane Ulo kneels in the shallows of his own tide, beaten, and takes off his helm. His hair is grey with salt. 'Thank you,' he says, and you do not understand, and then you do. He has been waiting a long time for someone to beat him. His tide goes back down {og_passage} without him, and for a moment he stays there, kneeling in nothing.

choices.text: Offer him a hand up

effects.log: He looks at your hand. He does not take it. He gets up on his own and walks after his tide, but he looks back once.

choices.text: Push the tide all the way back

effects.log: You push the tide down the passage. It goes easily, as if it had wanted to.

events.text: Thane Ulo is beaten, and he laughs: a short sea-sound, the first laugh you have heard from any of the Unborn that is not cruel. 'That is how my brother used to fight,' he says. 'Before.' He does not say before what. His Unborn stand around him in the grey water, waiting. 'Go home,' he tells them, and then, more quietly, 'what there is of it.'

choices.text: Ask about the brother

effects.log: He tells you a little. A brother who held a coast. A storm that was not a storm. Then he stops, and goes.

choices.text: Take the ground while he stands remembering

effects.log: You take it. He lets you. He seems to have forgotten you are there.

events.text: Ashkel stands over you on {og_passage} and offers you his hand, which is cool and dry. 'Do not take it personally,' he says, helping you up. 'Your world was always going to be eaten. I am only the one who happens to be holding the spoon.' His rows take another step. He pours you tea before he goes back to his table.

choices.text: Drink the tea. Learn his patience

effects.log: You drink it. It is bitter and very good. You find you have learned something about waiting.

choices.text: Pour the tea out on his step

effects.log: You pour it out. He sighs, as at a waste. 'Again, then,' he says, quite kindly.

events.text: You lie on the marble of {og_passage} looking up at a white parasol. Ashkel has not even stood up from his table. He beat you sitting down, with one hand, while pouring with the other, and now he is reading a book. 'Rest,' he says, without looking up. 'There is no hurry. There has never been any hurry.'

choices.text: Get up and walk back to your line

effects.log: You get up. It takes a long time. He turns a page while you do it.

choices.text: Stay on the marble, and do not give him the step

effects.log: You stay where you fell, and so the step is still yours. He looks at you over his book, amused, and lets you.

events.text: The Twins beat you together, which they have not done before: for one breath they are one sun again, and you cannot look at it. Afterwards, while you lie in the scorched grass, you hear them arguing over which of them did it. Ves says it was Ves. Ru says nothing. Ru, you realise, is glad.

choices.text: Remember how they joined

effects.log: You remember it: the moment each of them let go of the quarrel. You will know it if it comes again.

choices.text: Crawl back to your line in the dark

effects.log: You crawl. It is slow and ugly and nobody sees. You are back by morning.

events.text: Ves knocks you down and stands over you shouting, gold and furious, about how small you are. Then Ru, behind, says your name, very quietly, as though it were a word Ru had been learning. Ves stops. Ves turns to stare at Ru. You get up and go while they are still staring at each other.

choices.text: Wonder where Ru learned your name

effects.log: You wonder all night. You do not like any of the answers, and you like one of them very much.

choices.text: Turn back at the edge and take one step of ground

effects.log: You stop at the edge of the field and take one step back. It is not much. It is yours.

events.text: Old Moth folds you into her wings, very gently, and for a while you are a child again in a warm room with someone humming. When she lets you go you are on {og_passage}, alone, and you cannot remember a prayer you were sure you knew. 'There, now,' she says from somewhere above. 'Wasn't that nice?'

choices.text: Find the prayer again

effects.log: It takes a year. You find it in the mouth of a child in a far temple. You hold on to it very tightly.

choices.text: Go straight back to your temples

effects.log: You go back and say your name to the faithful until they say it back. The prayer can wait.

events.text: You lose to Old Moth in the dark of {og_passage}, and as you fall she says, quite sadly, 'Oh, you poor dear. You are so very thin. Nobody has been praying for you lately, have they?' It is true. While you fought her she was eating your faithful's prayers, and you have been fighting on an empty stomach.

choices.text: Go down and be prayed to, before the next fight

effects.log: You go down among your faithful. They pray, and you eat. It is not a dignified way for a god to recover.

choices.text: Fight her again tomorrow, hungry

effects.log: You fight hungry the next day as well. You lose again, but less. You learn what she does.

events.text: Karrow does not fight you. Karrow reads to you from the ledger, the worth of every world you might have saved, while the Unborn hold you down. It is the worst beating you have ever had. When it is over Karrow closes the book and says, 'Do not feel bad. Nobody has ever been worth more than they cost.'

choices.text: Remember the number Karrow gave you

effects.log: You remember it. You will prove it wrong. It is a very good number to hate.

choices.text: Laugh at Karrow, as you are carried off

effects.log: You laugh. Karrow writes something down, and frowns at it, and crosses it out.

events.text: Karrow beats you by the numbers, the way a tide beats a sandcastle: no great blow, only one after another after another, each exactly as large as it needs to be. When you are down, Karrow writes in the ledger, then tears out the page and gives it to you. 'Your receipt,' Karrow says.

choices.text: Read the receipt

effects.log: It lists, exactly, everything you did wrong. It is very useful. You hate that it is useful.

choices.text: Tear up the receipt in front of Karrow

effects.log: You tear it up. Karrow sighs. 'There is always a copy,' Karrow says.

events.text: The Bride beats you without touching you. She only opens a door in the air, and you look in, and it is your own hall, empty: no lamps, no servants, no you. While you look she walks past you up {og_passage}. When you come to yourself, the front has moved and she is sitting in a room of yours, looking around it with her veil up.

choices.text: Go back to your own hall and light every lamp

effects.log: You light them all. The hall is full again, and loud. You stand in it a long time.

choices.text: Ask her if this one feels like home

effects.log: She looks around your room and shakes her head. 'No,' she says. 'Not this one either.' She sounds sorry for you.

events.text: You fall, and the Bride kneels beside you, and lifts her veil to look at you, and her face is kind. 'You have a home,' she says. 'I can see it on you. It must be so warm.' She means no harm. She has never meant any harm. Her Unborn take another hill of {og_passage} while she sits there, envying you.

choices.text: Tell her about your home

effects.log: You tell her. She listens like a child to a story. When she goes, she takes the hill but leaves the story.

choices.text: Get up, and take back what you can

effects.log: You get up and take back half the hill before night. She watches you do it, wistful.

events.text: Thane Ulo beats you in the surf of his own tide and holds you under the grey water just long enough to make his point, and then pulls you out and sets you on the shore of {og_passage}. 'I am sorry,' he says, and he plainly is. 'I cannot let you win. Not yet. They would know.' He goes back to his Unborn before you can ask who.

choices.text: Think about what he said: 'They would know'

effects.log: You think about it for a long time. Somebody is watching Ulo. Somebody he is afraid of.

choices.text: Spit out the salt and get back to your line

effects.log: You spit out the salt. It tastes of a sea that does not exist. You get back to your line.

events.text: Ulo wins, and does not take the ground he has won. He stands at the line where you fell and holds his tide there with both hands, like a man holding a door against a storm. His Unborn murmur behind him. 'Go home,' he says to you, without turning. 'Tell your gods the tide was slow today.' You go.

choices.text: Tell your gods the truth

effects.log: You tell them he held back. Some of them do not believe it. The ones who were on the line do.

choices.text: Tell your gods the tide was slow today

effects.log: You tell them. It is not quite a lie. Ulo, far off, seems to hear it.

events.text: You send to your pantheon, and your pantheon comes: down {og_passage} in a long bright line, its gods in their war-colours, its old ones grumbling, its young ones singing. You had not been sure they would. {og_unborn} watches them arrive and, for once, has nothing to say. By nightfall the field is a field of your own gods.

choices.text: Thank each god of the pantheon by name

effects.log: It takes a whole night. They pretend not to be moved. They are moved.

choices.text: Put them where the line is thinnest

effects.log: You put them on the worst ground, and they hold it. The Heavenly Dao counts them, and you, together.

events.text: Your pantheon's answer comes in the form of a single old god, sent alone, who walks up to your line, looks at {og_passage}, says 'Hm,' and walks out onto the field. You are about to shout. Then the Unborn in front of the old god begin to fall back, and keep falling back, and the old god is humming.

choices.text: Ask the old god who they are

effects.log: They tell you a name you have read in the oldest books. They are surprised you have read it. They are pleased.

choices.text: Follow the old god out onto the field

effects.log: You walk out behind them. Between you the field is cleared by noon. The old god says you will do.

events.text: Your pantheon sends what it has, which this year is not much: a handful of gods, a cart of war-gear, and a letter apologising for both. But the handful are good, and they do not apologise, and they go straight to {og_passage} and start fighting as if they had been born there. The letter is the only thing that was afraid.

choices.text: Burn the letter. Keep the gods

effects.log: You burn it. The gods see you do it and grin. They fight better for the next ten years.

choices.text: Write back to the pantheon: send more letters like these

effects.log: You write back that the handful were worth a host. It is read aloud in the pantheon's hall.

events.text: The pantheon comes, and with it come the faithful of every god in it: not to fight, but to pray, at the foot of {og_passage}, in a great murmuring crowd. The Unborn cannot bear it. {og_unborn} sends them forward against the praying crowd and they come apart in the noise like fog in a wind.

choices.text: Pray with them

effects.log: You kneel in the crowd and pray, which a god does not do. Nobody notices but the Heavenly Dao.

choices.text: Fight in front of the crowd

effects.log: You fight in front of them all day. They pray for you by name. It is very hard to lose with that at your back.

events.text: You send to your pantheon, and your pantheon sends back a letter. It is very long. It says that the pantheon has its own passages, its own wars, and its own feasts, and that it trusts you to manage. At the bottom someone has written, in a different hand, 'Sorry.' {og_unborn} has watched you read it.

choices.text: Fight on alone, then

effects.log: You fight on alone. It is a long season. You do not write to them again.

choices.text: Write back, coldly, and keep a copy

effects.log: You write back. You keep a copy. One day someone in that hall will have to read it aloud.

events.text: Your pantheon sends gods, and the gods come, and when they see {og_passage} and {og_unborn} on it they stop at the head of the passage and do not go down. They are not cowards. They are only gods who have never seen a world eaten, and you have. You watch them go home in the same long bright line they came in.

choices.text: Let them go. You will hold

effects.log: You let them go. You hold. It is not their passage. It is yours.

choices.text: Go after them and shame them

effects.log: You catch them at the Stair and say what you think. Two of them turn back. Two is something.

events.text: The pantheon sends one god only, a young one, too young, with a borrowed sword and a letter of introduction. They are brave and they are no use, and on the first day {og_unborn} nearly takes them. You spend the season keeping one young god alive instead of holding a passage. It is, you think, what the pantheon meant to send you: a reason to stay.

choices.text: Send the young god home, alive

effects.log: You send them home. They are furious with you. They live a very long time.

choices.text: Teach them to hold a passage

effects.log: You teach them. By the end of the season they are some use. By the end of the war they are a lot.

events.text: Old Moth comes up {og_passage} for her supper and finds it shut against her with prayer: every temple below has lit every lamp, and the passage is full of their light from wall to wall. She flutters at the edge of it like a moth at a window. 'Oh, that is unkind,' she says, in her grandmother's voice. 'That is very unkind, dear.' She is starving, and she knows it.

choices.text: Keep the lamps lit until she goes

effects.log: You keep them lit for a year. She goes in the end, thin and querulous, down into the dark.

choices.text: Go to the edge and tell her to go home

effects.log: You tell her. She looks at you with her round grey eyes. 'I have no home, dear,' she says, and goes.

events.text: You seal {og_passage} with faith: every temple of yours, in every world below, praying the same prayer at the same hour. It is not a ward. It is a voice, a great one, and the passage fills with it. {og_unborn} stands on the far side and listens and cannot come through. The faithful will never know they held a war shut.

choices.text: Answer every one of them in return

effects.log: You answer them all, in small ways: a mended roof, a found ring. It takes a century. They held the passage; you owe them.

choices.text: Hold the seal yourself until it sets

effects.log: You hold it while it sets. It is like holding up a roof. The Heavenly Dao counts the hours.

events.text: The seal of faith goes up over {og_passage} like frost over a window, and you watch it set. It is made of a million small prayers, and you can hear some of them if you listen: a sick mother, a lost goat, a good harvest, please, a good harvest. Not one of them is about the Unborn. That is why it holds.

choices.text: Listen to the prayers for a while

effects.log: You listen for a day. You answer the goat one first. You are not sure why.

choices.text: Let the seal speak for itself, and go

effects.log: You go. Behind you {og_unborn} paces the far side of the frost for a long time.

events.text: You ask your faithful to pray, and they pray, and the seal on {og_passage} takes. But faith is a thing that is spent, and afterwards your temples are quiet and tired, and some of them are a little less sure of you. The Unborn are shut out. The cost is inside.

choices.text: Go down to the temples and rest them

effects.log: You visit every temple. You do not ask for anything. They are sure of you again by the next festival.

choices.text: Leave them to recover in their own time

effects.log: They recover in their own time. It is a long time. You learn patience from it.

events.text: The faith rises, and the passage shuts, and {og_unborn}, on the far side, bows to you through the seal, as one bows to a worthy enemy at the end of a game neither of you wanted. Then the commander turns and walks away into the dark. The seal will hold for a while. A while, in the heavens, is a long time. It is not forever.

choices.text: Bow back, through the seal

effects.log: You bow back. Neither of you is sure what you have agreed to. It feels like a promise.

choices.text: Turn your back on it, and get to work

effects.log: You turn your back and start on the next field. The seal will hold. You will not.

events.text: You go cap in hand to a pantheon that is not yours, which costs you standing, and ask for help at {og_passage}. They let you wait in their hall a long time. Then their eldest comes out and says, 'We had thought you too proud to ask.' They come. It is the first time their banner and yours have flown side by side.

choices.text: Fly the two banners together after the war, too

effects.log: You keep them side by side. It is the beginning of an old friendship, late.

choices.text: Give them the place of honour on the line

effects.log: You give them the best of the line and the most dangerous. They hold it. The Heavenly Dao counts both pantheons.

events.text: A rival pantheon, one that has fought yours for ten thousand years, answers your asking by sending its champion: a god you once beat in a duel for a domain. They walk up to you on {og_passage}, look at you, and say, 'I would rather lose to you than to that.' Then they turn to face {og_unborn}.

choices.text: Fight beside them, and do not mention the old duel

effects.log: You fight side by side. Neither of you mentions it. Afterwards, at the fire, you both do, and laugh.

choices.text: Fight beside them, and take the field

effects.log: Together you take the whole field by night. It is the best fight of your life, and it is not against each other.

events.text: You ask, and the asking is humbling: you go to the halls of three pantheons and say plainly that you cannot hold {og_passage} alone. Two of them say no. The third, the smallest, says yes, and sends everyone it has. It is not many. It is everyone. The other two will hear of it.

choices.text: Remember the third, always

effects.log: You remember. When the war is over, the third pantheon finds it has a friend at every council.

choices.text: Put the small pantheon's gods where they will be seen

effects.log: You put them where everyone will see them hold. They hold. The Heavenly Dao sees too.

events.text: The pantheon you ask sends an old enemy of yours, a god of the Silent Hall who has never forgiven you for something you barely remember. They arrive at {og_passage}, look at {og_unborn}, look at you, and say, 'I will forgive you for the duration.' They mean it. They are terrifying on the field.

choices.text: Ask, finally, what you did to them

effects.log: They tell you. It was a small cruelty, a thousand years ago. You apologise. They are startled into silence.

choices.text: Let them take the front, and follow

effects.log: You follow your old enemy into the Unborn ranks. They clear a road. You walk it.

events.text: You ask the other pantheons, and the asking costs you, and the answer is no. Not rudely. They are sorry. They have read about the Unborn, and they think the Unborn will stop at your passages, and they have decided not to be the next. You walk home past their halls and see them putting up wards of their own.

choices.text: Tell them, coldly, that the Unborn do not stop

effects.log: You tell them. They know. They do it anyway. You go home.

choices.text: Say nothing. You will need them later

effects.log: You say nothing and thank them for their time. Later, when you need them, they will remember it.

events.text: A pantheon says it will come, and does not come. You wait at {og_passage} for three days with the line thin and {og_unborn} watching you wait. On the fourth day their envoy arrives, alone, very sorry, to say there has been a difficulty. You do not ask what. You can see it in the envoy's face: they were afraid.

choices.text: Send the envoy home kindly

effects.log: You send the envoy home with a gift. It is not their fault their masters are afraid.

choices.text: Make the envoy stay and fight

effects.log: The envoy stays. They are afraid, too, and they fight anyway. They are the bravest god of that whole pantheon.

events.text: You go to the Will of Heaven, the proudest of the pantheons, and ask, and they make you kneel to ask. You kneel. They take a long time to answer, and when they answer it is no, and they have made you kneel for it. The whole heavens hear of it by evening. {og_unborn} hears of it too.

choices.text: Stand up, and never kneel again

effects.log: You stand up. Your knees are not the thing that is hurt. You go back to the passage.

choices.text: Thank them for their time, kneeling

effects.log: You thank them from your knees. It is such a strange thing that some of their own gods come to you secretly that night.

events.text: The field at {og_passage} closes, the way a wound closes, and you were not there. Something else held you, a council or a duel or a quarrel over a domain, and while you were busy {og_unborn} took what the Unborn came for and went. There was no battle. There is no one to blame. There is a little less of the passage than there was.

choices.text: Go and stand where the field was

effects.log: You stand there. It is quiet, and smaller. You promise the quiet you will not be busy next time.

choices.text: Ask who did fight, while you were not there

effects.log: Two minor gods did, alone. You find them and thank them. They did not expect to be thanked.

events.text: No one answered the field at {og_passage}. You did not; your pantheon did not; the other halls did not. The Unborn walked up it and walked down again, carrying what they came for. Below, in the worlds the passage leads to, people woke one morning a little more frightened than they had gone to sleep, and did not know why.

choices.text: Go down and find what was taken

effects.log: You go down. What was taken was hard to name: a feeling of being watched over. You stay a while to put it back.

choices.text: Resolve that this will not happen twice

effects.log: You make a list of every god who should have answered. Your own name is first.

events.text: You hear of the field after it closed, from a messenger who arrived too late at the wrong hall. {og_unborn} had come up {og_passage} and stood on it for a season, waiting, as if waiting for an answer. When none came, the commander took the front a little closer and went, and left a note. The note says, 'Next time.'

choices.text: Keep the note

effects.log: You keep it. Next time, you will be there.

choices.text: Punish the slow messenger

effects.log: You punish them, and then you are ashamed. The messenger was only slow. You were not there either.

events.text: The front at {og_passage} moved while you looked the other way. It does not seem to matter much. A step, a hill. But you have seen what the Unborn do with steps and hills, given time, and you know it matters. You count what was lost, as Karrow would, and the count is small, and the count is not the point.

choices.text: Go to the front and take back the step

effects.log: You go. You take the step back by yourself, in a night. It matters.

choices.text: Sit with the count, and learn from it

effects.log: You sit with it. You learn something about yourself you did not want to.

events.text: Ashkel the Unweeping is beaten a second time, and this time he does not get up. He sits on the step of {og_passage} with his torn parasol across his knees and looks at the sky of your world for a long while, as if reading it. 'I wrote that you were eaten,' he says at last. 'I shall have to write something else. What shall I write?'

choices.text: Write the ending yourself: he does not leave

effects.log: You end him on the step, quickly and with courtesy, as he would have wished. The parasol is all that is left. You keep it.

choices.text: Tell him to write that he went home

effects.log: He considers it. 'I have none,' he says, 'but I shall write it.' He goes into the dark without his parasol, and does not come back.

events.text: The second time, Ashkel loses quickly, and seems almost relieved. He pours two cups at his table on {og_passage}, sets one in front of you, and folds his hands. 'In nine thousand worlds,' he says, 'nobody has made me hurry. You have made me hurry twice. I find I do not want to go on.' He waits, politely, for your answer.

choices.text: Drink with him, and then end it

effects.log: You drink together. Then you end it. He bows his head to make it easier for you.

choices.text: Leave the tea undrunk, and tell him to go

effects.log: You leave the cup. He bows, takes his parasol, and walks back into the dark. In the far distance it closes, slowly, and is gone.

events.text: The Twins are beaten twice, and this time they cannot pull apart: they lie in the grass of {og_passage} as one dim sun, gold and pale at once, and both voices come out of it. 'Put me out,' says Ves. 'Put me out,' says Ru. 'Not the other.' 'Not the other.' They have never agreed on anything before. They are agreeing now.

choices.text: Put them out together. Neither is left alone

effects.log: You put out the sun. It goes gently, both halves at once, and there is a moment of perfect quiet in which nobody is quarrelling.

choices.text: Put neither out. Send the one sun away

effects.log: You step back. The dim sun rises, slowly, and drifts off into the dark, gold and pale, and for once in silence.

events.text: Ves lies beaten, and Ru stands between Ves and you, pale fire shaking, and speaks a whole sentence at last: 'I was the half that let our world die. Ves only shouted. Take me.' Behind, Ves is trying to get up, and shouting that Ru is a liar, that it was Ves, it was always Ves, take Ves.

choices.text: Take neither alone: end the Twins together

effects.log: You end them together, which is the only mercy you can think of. The last thing you hear is the two of them, still arguing.

choices.text: Let them both go, on condition they never return

effects.log: They swear it, in two voices that for once say the same words. They go. They keep the oath.

events.text: Old Moth, beaten twice, is no bigger than a lamp-moth, and she has no strength left to flutter. She lies in your palm on {og_passage}, grey and soft, and says, 'I was a goddess of the hearth once, dear. The hearth went out. I have only ever been hungry since.' Her wings tremble. She is not asking for anything.

choices.text: Close your hand, gently

effects.log: You close your hand. When you open it there is only a little grey dust, and the smell of a kitchen on a winter evening.

choices.text: Put her down by a temple lamp, and walk away

effects.log: You set her by a lamp. She looks at it a long time. When you look back, she is gone, and the lamp is burning a little brighter.

events.text: The second time you beat Old Moth, every prayer she ever ate in your heavens comes up out of her at once, a cloud of them, ten thousand years of small requests. She looks up at them going. 'They were lovely,' she says. 'All of them. Thank you for letting me hear them.' Then she waits, quite calmly, for whatever you will do.

choices.text: End her while the prayers rise

effects.log: You end her in the cloud of prayers. Afterwards you answer as many of them as you can, as though for her.

choices.text: Let her go, and keep the prayers

effects.log: You let her go. She goes slowly, like an old woman going home from market. The prayers stay with you.

events.text: Karrow, beaten twice, sits on the ground of {og_passage} with the great ledger open and goes through it, page by page, nine thousand worlds. 'I always settle,' Karrow says. 'What do I owe you?' It is a real question. Karrow will pay whatever you name. You can see the number being worked out behind the spectacles.

choices.text: Name the price: Karrow, and the ledger

effects.log: Karrow nods, as though it were fair. You end them both. The ledger burns very slowly, a world at a time.

choices.text: Name the price: go, and stop counting

effects.log: Karrow stares. Then, slowly, closes the ledger, and leaves it on the ground, and walks away into the dark without it.

events.text: The second defeat seems to astonish Karrow more than the first. 'Twice,' Karrow says, 'twice,' and begins writing the word in the margin, over and over, as though it might add up. The Unborn are gone; only Karrow is left on {og_passage}, with the desk, the scale and the pen. You can end it. You can leave Karrow writing forever.

choices.text: End it. Close the book

effects.log: You close it. Karrow does not resist. The last thing Karrow writes is your name, with no question mark.

choices.text: Take the pen, and leave Karrow alone

effects.log: You take the pen. Karrow looks at the empty hand for a long time. Then gets up, and goes, and has nothing to count.

events.text: The Bride is beaten twice, and kneels on {og_passage} with her veil torn. Around her, in the air, the doors she opened stand open on empty rooms, hundreds of them, as far as you can see. 'I only wanted one,' she says. 'Just one that was mine.' You think of your heavens, which are wide, and full of halls nobody uses.

choices.text: End her, and close the rooms

effects.log: You end it gently. The rooms close one after another, like a house at night, until the air is clear.

choices.text: Let her go back to her searching

effects.log: You let her go. She goes on into the dark, opening doors, looking in, sighing, as she always has.

choices.text: Give her a home. A hall of your own, empty, hers
